[MUJAHID:v2p507/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | He reports that the sage Luqman worked as a tailor.
[MUQATIL:31:12-13/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Luqman’s son was named Anʿum; he counseled him against shirk, the gravest injustice, and his son and wife eventually became Muslim through persistence.
[MUQATIL:31:12-13/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · قتادة بن دعامة | reports | Qatada reports that Luqman was flat-nosed and from Abyssinia.
[MUQATIL:31:12-13/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · الهذيل | reports | Hudhayl says he did not hear Muqatil report the preceding description.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p673/r2] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | Luqman warns his son against shirk because it wrongs and harms the person who commits it; Hasan says it diminishes oneself, and al-Suddi calls it a great sin.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p673/r3] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · ابن مسعود | reports | When 6:82 said believers had not mixed faith with injustice, the Companions asked who was free of injustice; 31:13 was revealed to identify shirk as the injustice meant. | mentions 6:82
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p673/r4] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet describes three wrongs: shirk is unforgiven, sins between a servant and God may be forgiven, and wrongs between people are not left without reciprocal redress.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p157/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | إذ may be extra in the cited clauses from 2:30 and 31:13, where the sense is simply “and He said.”
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p157/r5] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | He also cites Ibn Mayyada's line beginning إذ لا يزال as poetic evidence for the extra use of إذ.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p258/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The basic Arab sense of ẓulm is placing something outside its proper place; common expressions apply it to resemblance, premature drinking, needless slaughter, wrongly dug land, and leaving a road.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p258/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | Ẓulm can mean shirk because assigning God a partner places lordship where it does not belong; this is also the sense of the cited verse in al-Anʿām. | mentions 6:82
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p258/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | Ẓulm also means diminution or withholding: the cited phrases about crops, rights, and souls mean that nothing was reduced or withheld. | mentions 2:57, 18:33, 19:60, 36:54
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p258/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | Ẓulm can mean denial: the Thamūd denied that the she-camel was from God, and “wronging Our signs” means denying them. | mentions 17:59, 7:9
[TAB-FULL:v18p550/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | God tells Muhammad to recall Luqman's counsel to his son: do not associate partners with God, since shirk is a grave error in speech.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p195#2/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | إذ is governed by ‘We gave Luqman wisdom’: God gave it to him when he admonished his son, since this admonition itself is wisdom.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p195#2/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Shirk is grave injustice because God alone gives life, death, provision, and blessings; assigning a blessing to another is placing it with the wrong giver.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p195#2/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The basic Arabic meaning of ظلم is putting something in the wrong place.
[NAHHAS:v3p283/r7] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | إذ is accusative with an understood command to remember; Abu Ishaq instead attaches it to the gift of wisdom, which al-Nahhas rejects because of the wāw and word order.
[NAHHAS:v3p283/r8] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | يا بني has kasra on yāʾ to indicate omitted yāʾ; some give fatḥa because it is lighter.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p453#2/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathir's Ibn Abi Bizza transmission uses silent yāʾ in يا بني لا تشرك, kasra in يا بني إنها, and fatḥa in يا بني أقم; Qunbul has silence in the first and third and kasra in the middle. | mentions 31:16, 31:17
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p453#2/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · حفص عن عاصم | reports | Hafs from Asim reads all three يا بني forms with fatḥa; Abu Bakr from Asim, Nafi, Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Hamza, and Kisai use kasra in the third form. | mentions 31:16, 31:17
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p453#2/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · المفضل عن عاصم | reports | Al-Mufaddal from Asim reads يا بني with fatḥa in all three cited places. | mentions 31:16, 31:17
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p453#2/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | A silent yāʾ in connected recitation extends a pause form into speech, an extension known in poetry but not ordinary speech; a kasra form is the normal vocative construction because the possessive yāʾ acts like tanwīn and drops. | mentions 31:16
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p453#2/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Fatḥa on the yāʾ comes from يا بنيا, replacing the possessive yāʾ with alif and changing kasra to fatḥa; Abu Uthman explains يا أبت similarly. | mentions 19:42
[SULAMI:v2p130#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Luqman's first counsel against associating partners with God is to single out the Real with one's whole self, heart, and spirit, serving and seeing none but Him.
[SULAMI:v2p130#2/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · محمد بن علي | reports | Admonition is calling people to the Real and His way.
[THALABI:v7p320/r16] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The warning against arguing about God without knowledge was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who claimed the angels were God's daughters.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p333/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Muhammad is told to recall Luqman's admonition to his son; the son is variously named Mishkam, An'am, or Baban.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p333/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Luqman was reminding and disciplining his son; calling him يا بني conveys tenderness, not literal diminutiveness.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p333/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Shirk is immense injustice because the idolater wrongs himself before God.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p16#2/r25] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Shirk is divided into overt idolatry and hidden shirk, which includes attributing events to created people or affirming another alongside God while witnessing the unseen.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p16#2/r26] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Another definition calls shirk affirming anything other than God while witnessing the unseen.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p16#2/r27] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Shirk wrongs the heart, whereas sins wrong the self; wrongs of the self may be forgiven, but there is no avenue to forgiveness for wronging the heart.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p101#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq parses idh as an accusative linked to God giving Luqmān wisdom: the wisdom was given when he admonished his son, since the admonition itself is wisdom.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p101#2/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās takes the admonition to concern God.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p101#2/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | Muqātil says Luqmān’s son and wife were unbelievers, and he kept admonishing them until they became Muslims.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p101#2/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathīr reads yā bunayya with a lightened, still yāʾ and sukūn, also reported for the address at the start of verse 17. | mentions 31:17
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p101#2/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | He explains the reading as reducing the shadda after deleting the possessive yāʾ from the original three yāʾs; he considers other reading explanations preferable and says such lightening fits a verse-ending rhyme better.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p101#2/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | He defends treating the final yāʾ as still present in underlying grammar even when eased at a pause, citing a poetic form with the yāʾ of banī lightened and its non-restoration in the plural as evidence.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p101#2/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | He notes that the lightened reading is pronounced as though pause-form were carried into connected speech, as in the cited poetic examples.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p103/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says no sin is greater than associating a partner with God.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p103/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq reasons that God alone gives life, death, sustenance, and blessings; assigning worship to another misplaces the blessing and is thus the greatest injustice.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p103/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Linguistically, injustice is putting something somewhere it does not belong.
[JISHUMI:v8p5649/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathīr has several transmitted vocalizations for “my son”; the author identifies one as the relied-upon set and notes the many variants.
[JISHUMI:v8p5649/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · حفص عن عاصم | reports | Ḥafṣ opens the yāʾ of “my son” throughout the Qur'an; the other readers use kasra. Sukun follows the original form, fatḥa drops the possessive after three yāʾs, and kasra is close to the possessive form.
[JISHUMI:v8p5649/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو مسلم | reports | “When Luqman said to his son” coordinates with the account of wisdom, as if he was given wisdom when commanded to thank God and when admonishing his son; “while admonishing him” is circumstantial accusative.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p287/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | Luqman's son was called Anam, or, according to another report, Mashkam.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p287/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | For ya bunayya la tushrik, Ibn Kathir reads the yāʾ quiescent, Hafs with fatḥa, and the others with kasra; other ya bunayya forms in nearby counsel also vary by reader.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p500#2/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · قيل | reports | One report names Luqman's son An'am.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p500#2/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbi instead gives Luqman's son's name as Ashkam.

F-FULL:v3p500#2/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · قيل | reports | Another report says Luqman's son and wife were unbelievers, but Luqman kept persuading them until they accepted Islam.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p500#2/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Shirk is an immense injustice because it equates the sole giver of blessings with one who gives none and cannot give any; the enormity is beyond conception.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p347#2/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Idh qāla may mean remember when Luqman said it, or We granted him wisdom when he said it; the wording is shortened because the preceding context makes it clear.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p347#2/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Luqman's son was named Tharan.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p347#2/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · نافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي وأبو بكر عن عاصم | reports | These readers double the yāʾ and give it kasra in the three occurrences of yā bunayya; Hafs and al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿAsim double it with fatḥa.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p347#2/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن أبي برة عن ابن كثير وقنبل | reports | Ibn Abi Barra reports Ibn Kathir with a silent yāʾ in the first occurrence, kasra in the second, and fatḥa in the third; Qunbul reports silence in the first and third and kasra in the second.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p347#2/r14] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The warning that shirk is grave injustice may be Luqman's own speech or a divine statement attached to it; the report about 6:82 supports the latter and says it calmed the Companions' alarm. | mentions 6:82
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p348/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The Companions' concern could be eased if the phrase were God's own statement; it could also be eased by God quoting a servant already described as wise and sound. | mentions 6:82
[TABRISI:31:11-14/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن كثير برواية البزي | reports | Al-Bazzī's Ibn Kathīr transmission varies the ya in yā bunayya: sukūn in the prohibition, kasra in annahā, and fatḥa in the prayer command.
[TABRISI:31:11-14/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · القواس | reports | The al-Qawwās transmission has sukūn in the prohibition and prayer vocatives, and kasra in annahā.
[TABRISI:31:11-14/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن فليح | reports | Ibn Fulayḥ has sukūn in the first vocative, kasra in annahā, and fatḥa in the prayer vocative.
[TABRISI:31:11-14/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · حفص | reports | Ḥafṣ reads yā bunayya with fatḥa throughout the Qur'an; the remaining readers use kasra throughout.
[TABRISI:31:11-14/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي | holds | A reader who suppresses the yāʾ may be applying a pause form in connected speech, as in poetry that shortens jān for rhyme and then links it.
[TABRISI:31:11-14/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي | holds | The kasra in yā bunayya annahā follows the form yā ghulāmi aqbil; fatḥa treats the added yāʾ as changed to an alif, like yā abati according to Abu ʿUthman.
[TABRISI:31:11-15#2/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · لقمان | reports | Travel counsel says pray as soon as prayer time begins, preferably in congregation; do not sleep on an animal except in a litter that lets the limbs relax, and feed it before yourself near home.
[TABRISI:31:11-15#2/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · لقمان | reports | At a campsite choose pleasant, soft, grassy ground, pray two cycles before sitting, go far away for relieving yourself, then pray two and greet the place and its angelic residents when leaving.
[TABRISI:31:11-15#2/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · لقمان | reports | Give some food away before eating if possible; recite scripture while riding, praise God while working, pray when alone, avoid traveling through the whole night, and do not raise your voice on the road.
[TABRISI:31:11-15/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Luqman's master asked him to slaughter a sheep and bring its two best morsels; Luqman brought the heart and tongue, saying they are best when good and worst when bad.
[TABRISI:31:11-15/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Luqman warned that sitting too long on the toilet harms the liver, causes hemorrhoids, and heats the head; sit and rise gently, so the master wrote this wisdom on the privy door.
[TABRISI:31:11-15/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · عبد الله بن دينار | reports | On returning from travel, Luqman heard that his father, wife, sister, and brother had died; he responded respectively that he now controlled his affairs, renewed his bed, covered his nakedness, and had lost his support.
[TABRISI:31:11-15/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · لقمان | reports | Asked who is worst, Luqman answered: one unconcerned that people see him doing wrong.
[TABRISI:31:11-15/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · لقمان | reports | When someone called his face ugly, he asked whether the criticism was of the design or its designer.
[TABRISI:31:11-15/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · لقمان | reports | Luqman watched David forge armor, praised it as good battle clothing, and said silence is wisdom few practice; David affirmed that Luqman deserved his name.
[TABRISI:31:11-15/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · لقمان | reports | A counsel in Man lā yaḥḍuruhu al-faqīh likens the world to a deep sea where many perish: make faith the ship, trust in God its sail, and piety its provisions.
[TABRISI:31:11-15/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عبد الله | reports | Abu ʿAbdillah's travel counsel calls for necessary gear and medicine, agreeable companions except in sin, frequent consultation, smiling, sharing food, helping companions, silence, prayer, and generosity with mounts, water, and provisions.
[TABRISI:31:11-15/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عبد الله | reports | His counsel says to verify advice before deciding, help and work alongside companions, heed elders, answer requests graciously, stop and deliberate when lost, and distrust solitary strangers in the wilderness as possible scouts or devils.
[TABRISI:31:14/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Remember when Luqman spoke to his son may attach either to the command to remember or to God's giving him wisdom.
[TABRISI:31:14/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The diminutive bunayya expresses tenderness and compassion, not belittlement; Luqman warns his son not to associate anything with God in worship.
[TABRISI:31:14/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Shirk is grave injustice because injustice is withholding what is due: the polytheist denies God's due, knowledge of His oneness; it also ruins the self.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p371/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutayba describes shirk linguistically as a verbal noun meaning to partner with someone in a matter.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p371/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · معاذ | reports | The entry cites a hadith report that Muadh permitted partnership among people of Yemen.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p371/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | In sharecropping, shirk can mean two or three people entering into a partnership.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p371/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Shirk with God means assigning Him a partner.
[RAZI-FULL:v25p128/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Luqman begins with the most important counsel, forbidding associationism because it is grave injustice.
[RAZI-FULL:v25p128/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Shirk wrongs the honored human by directing worship to a base object or by placing worship where it does not belong; it is uniquely grave because no one besides God can be worshipped. | mentions 17:70
[QURTUBI-FULL:31:13/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · السهيلي | reports | Al-Suhaylī says Luqmān's son was called Thārān according to al-Ṭabarī and al-Qutbī.
[QURTUBI-FULL:31:13/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbī names Luqmān's son as Mishkam.
[QURTUBI-FULL:31:13/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النقاش | reports | Al-Naqqāsh transmits another name for the son: Anʿam.
[QURTUBI-FULL:31:13/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · القشيري | reports | Al-Qushayrī says Luqmān's son and wife were unbelievers, and he continued admonishing them until they accepted Islam.
[QURTUBI-FULL:31:13/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The admonition against associating partners with God supports the claim that Luqmān was instructing his son.
[QURTUBI-FULL:31:13/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | When 6:82 was revealed, the Companions feared that any wrongdoing invalidated their faith; the Prophet clarified that the verse's ظلم means shirk, as Luqmān told his son. | mentions 6:82
[QURTUBI-FULL:31:13/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Scholars differ whether the statement that shirk is grave injustice is Luqmān's words or a divine comment joined to them; the reported revelation supports the latter, though either attribution could reassure the Companions. | mentions 6:82
[QURTUBI-FULL:31:13/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The particle idh is accusative as an instruction to remember; al-Zajjāj instead attaches it to āṯaynā, but al-Naḥḥās considers that mistaken because the intervening wāw prevents it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:31:13/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The address yā bunayya is read with kasra on the yāʾ to indicate an omitted yāʾ; some use fatḥa as lighter. Its diminutive form expresses tenderness, not literal smallness.
[QURTUBI-FULL:6:81-82/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | When the Companions feared that every wrong disqualified them, the Prophet explained the verse by citing Luqman's statement that associating partners with God is grave injustice. | mentions 31:13
[BAYDAWI-FULL:31:13-16/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The source gives several possible names for Luqman's son: Anʿam, Ashkam, or another uncertain name.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:31:13-16/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Ya bunayya is a diminutive expressing tenderness; Ibn Kathir, Hafs, al-Bazzi, and other readers differ on its yāʾ vowel in the cited places. | mentions 31:17
